_about.what: The war at sea. Fleets are counts of ships by class. A fleet on patrol holds a sea: it fights enemy fleets there, guards convoys and stops enemy troopships. A fleet raiding hunts merchant ships and avoids battle. A fleet in port is safe and refits.
_about.classes: power is a ship's weight in a fleet action. tough scales how likely it is to be sunk when its fleet takes losses (lower is tougher). escort is its worth guarding a convoy, raid its worth hunting one.
_about.quality: How well a navy fights, ship for ship.
_about.air: Aircraft flying from a sea's coasts count toward holding it. weight turns air strength into fleet strength. A surface fleet at sea where the enemy's air outweighs its own by more than 'safe' loses ships to bombers every month: lossPer of the fleet for each point beyond that, up to maxLoss. A computer-run admiral keeps out of water where the margin is over 'avoid'.
_about.closed: A sea is closed to a nation's troopships and supply ships when the enemy's strength there (ships at sea plus aircraft) is at least 'min' and at least 'ratio' times its own.
_about.ready: A fleet in harbour regains 'port' of its fitness for sea each month. On patrol it wears down to 'floor' and no further, and a damaged fleet that stays out mends only slowly. A battle costs the loser 'lost' and the winner 'won'. A computer-run fleet that has gone in to refit comes out again at sortieAt.
_about.battle: A patrolling fleet offers battle when it is at least 'seek' times as strong as the enemy in its sea. Raiding surface ships are brought to action with chance catchRaider. A fleet outnumbered by evadeAt or more slips away to port with chance evade.
_about.watch: The coast watch's report (the grand campaign). When a nation's month closes with 'corps' or more of its field corps standing idle on a quay, shipping for as many, and an enemy's home coast within a landing's range over seas open to its troopships, that enemy's coast watch reports it: his staff mans its harbours and a player is warned. Only a corps that has not moved in the month can embark, so the report is always a month ahead of the landing. The same quay is reported again only after 'every' months.
_about.intercept: Troopships crossing a sea where enemy ships or aircraft are at work lose men: up to 'loss' of a corps when the enemy is unopposed. 'sea' is how hard a convoy is to find.
_about.landing: A corps landing on a defended coast fights at 'assault' strength; in the month war is declared the defenders are caught unready and it fights at 'surprise' strength and cannot be intercepted. range is how many seas a landing force can cross. Enemy fleets in harbour on those seas or the next ones put to sea against an invasion at 'sortie' of their strength. No landing can be made under a sky the enemy's fighters still hold, unless it is a surprise. Airborne troops (corps marked 'airborne' in the setup) need no ships and no open sea lane: once a month they can be flown from a friendly coast to an enemy one across a single sea, and fight there at 'airborne' strength, without heavy weapons. craft lists, as [from turn, nations, strength], who has purpose-built landing ships and the naval gunfire to cover a beach, and from when: their assaults fight at that strength instead of 'assault'.
_about.convoys: Routes that feed a nation by sea. The share of the cargo lost is raiders / (raiders + escorts x escortWorth + ocean); 'share' of the nation's production rides on the route, and 'tons' is the shipping sunk in a month if nothing got through. 'base' is a fortress astride the route: while an enemy of the route's owner holds it, its own submarines and aircraft hunt the convoys with strength 'raid', or 'starved' of that when it is cut off itself. What is sunk on the Libya route also lengthens the supply line of the armies in the desert: see desert.json.
_about.ore: Swedish iron ore reaches Germany across the Baltic when it is free of ice, and down the Norwegian coast from Narvik when it is not. If neither way is open, Germany loses 'share' of her production.
_about.fleets: The navies of 1 September 1939. base is the region of the home port (null for a base off the map, with 'home' naming the sea it opens on) and port its name. zone is the sea the fleet is stationed in and duty what it does there. 'from' brings a fleet into being later in the war. 'open' holds what the row says instead in the grand campaign: Force H is at home in Gibraltar with the Western Mediterranean as its beat, tied to it, as the historian has it (historian/italian-boats-b562.md, part 2: the western Mediterranean first, the near Atlantic only for dated events; ruling 233 rider b564). The history campaigns keep the row as it was. 'book' holds the month and the ships a row forms with instead at those stops of the grand campaign, for the computer's navy only, as every row of the dial: at stops 1 and 2 Force H forms at turn 10 (June 1940), with the Resolution, the Ark Royal, the Arethusa and 9 destroyers (the Ark Royal leaves the Home Fleet by the arrivals that month, and the Resolution is in no first-day row, so she comes from off the chart), and the Hood and the Valiant come to it from the Home Fleet by the arrivals (historian/italian-boats-b562.md, part 2 and its addendum of 19 November, Force H's first months; ruling 233, the director's note of 10:06Z). Where the dial reaches one of its stops only after that month, the fleet forms in the first month at one of them, up to its own month. Everywhere else, the history campaigns and the player's own navy included, Force H forms at turn 11 with its own row's ships, as before. A fleet 'tied' to its home and its beat, which the computer's admirals send nowhere else, loses the tie the month its home port falls, or once its beat is out of reach from the port it is in, and from then its admiral places it as any other fleet: every tied fleet, in every campaign (ruling 233 rider b598).
_about.building: Ships that join a fleet every month over a span of turns.
_about.arrivals: Single ships that join a fleet in a given month: [turn, nation, fleet, ships, what the news calls them]. A count below none is ships leaving. A sixth entry, where there is one, dates the row by the history dial: 'stops' are the grand campaign's stops it is read at (never in a history campaign), and 'sunk' counts the ships that leave as lost. For the player's own navy such a row is read in the start month of a campaign begun later, as the computer's (the record's ships are the start position: ruling 234 rider b639); after that month the dial moves none of his ships, so a move ('from'), a departure or a row standing in for a plain one ('instead') is never read for him, but a ship coming onto the chart from off it comes to him on its row's date at its row's fleet, once (the director's note of 15:52Z, 19 November). 'back' marks a ship's return to the chart: [turn, fleet] of the row that sent her off it. For the player it is read only where that row was read for him, at his start, so that a ship whose leaving fell after his start, and which stayed with him, never comes twice; and it comes on its date whatever its 'waits', since a ship off the chart is no ship he can order. 'instead', on a dated row, names the turn of the plain row ('not') it stands in for: the player reads the plain row, so never this one. Such a row is read once, in the first month at one of its stops on or after its date: a grand campaign begun later, or a dial turned to the book later, has the record's ships of that month, and a row from before it changes them without news. 'not', on a row with no date of the dial, names the stops at which the computer's navy does not read it, a dated row standing in its place. 'from' makes a row a move: its ships come from that fleet of the same navy, as many of them as it has (none from a fleet that has lost them, and then no news), so no ship is in two fleets and none comes back from the bottom. 'waits' holds a row until play has taken from its fleet a ship of each kind it brings that no waiting row has yet made good, that is, until the fleet's losses are more than its waiting rows have brought: it is read in the first month on or after its date in which that is so, after the month's other rows, once and with its news; until then it is not read, however long. The game counts ships and never names them, so it is a carrier lost that a waiting row replaces, whichever she was. 'by', on a move, names the turn of the waiting row of 'from' that would bring those ships there: while that row has not been read they come from off the chart instead, and it is closed. 'fromIf' is a move from that fleet where it is on the chart in this game, and otherwise an arrival from off the chart, so that every ship is counted once: the Eagle's row of turn 9 brings her from the China Fleet when the far side is on, and from off the chart when it is not (its key is the row's own, as before). 'lapse' closes a row for good: from that turn on it is never read. 'most' is the most of each class named that the fleet may hold after the row: a row read late into a fleet that formed with those ships already (Force H formed by its own row, before the dial was turned to the book) brings no second of them. A waiting row lapses when the record's window for that posting closes (ruling 233, the director's notes of 10:02Z and 11:21Z): the Eagle's in the West at 36, when Pedestal's rows take over, and the Formidable's in the East at 21 (May 1941), so that the East never holds more than two fleet carriers at once. The carriers at stops 1 and 2 (ruling 233, the director's notes of 08:34Z and 08:38Z; the historian's addendum to historian/bordeaux-med-subs-b598.md): each fleet carrier's arrivals in and departures from the Mediterranean, 1939 to 1942, one row each way, the East being the Mediterranean Fleet and the West Force H. The Glorious out at 2 (October 1939, for the Indian Ocean), back at 5 and to the Home Fleet at 8 (Norway); the Eagle in the East at 9, out at 20 (the South Atlantic), and in the West from 30, waiting for the Ark Royal to go, until her row lapses at 36; the Ark Royal out of the Home Fleet at 10, the month Force H forms with her by its book (she reached Gibraltar about 23 June 1940 and Force H formed on 28 June, both in turn 10); Force H's first months (historian/italian-boats-b562.md, the addendum of 19 November; the director's note of 10:06Z): the battlecruiser Hood and the battleship Valiant from the Home Fleet at 10, the cruiser Enterprise and two destroyers at 11, the Hood home to the Home Fleet and the battlecruiser Renown in from off the chart at 12 (she is in no first-day row), and the Valiant east to the Mediterranean Fleet at 13 (Operation Hats), with two destroyers out of Force H that month, home for anti-invasion duty and to Dakar, so that it holds 9 from then, the top of the historian's 7 to 9 and its row's own (the director's note of 11:21Z: transfers, so a row); the Resolution torpedoed at Dakar at 13 is the battle's, so no row; the game counts a battlecruiser as a battleship ('bb'), as it counts the Repulse in the Home Fleet's; the Illustrious from the Home Fleet to the East at 13; the Formidable in the East from 19, waiting for the Illustrious to go, until her row lapses at 21, so that her row of turn 16 is not read there; the Furious's Malta ferry run, in the West at 21 and home at 22; Pedestal, the Victorious and the Furious in the West at 36 and home at 37; Torch, the Formidable, the Victorious and the Furious in the West at 39 (the Formidable from the East if she came there, and otherwise from off the chart) and the Victorious home at 40. The Indomitable and the Argus are on no fleet's roster and have no row. A departure the record owed to battle (the Illustrious and the Formidable bombed, the Ark Royal and the Eagle sunk, the Indomitable hit) is no row: the battle decides it. Two of the rows are read at every stop as facts of the day (historian/bordeaux-med-subs-b598.md, part 3; ruling 233 rider b601): the Glorious out at 2 and the Eagle in the East at 9. From stop 3 no other is read, and a carrier goes only if play sinks it.
_about.beats: Where a navy's submarines sail, by beat (ruling 233 rider b564; the historian's rows, historian/italian-boats-b562.md). Each group is a fleet: a group that gives only a name is the fleet of that name the navy already has (Italy's Submarine Fleet at La Spezia is the western beat), and the others are rows of their own, formed in the grand campaign the first month they have boats, with a line of news. 'held' is a place the group sails from only while the nation or an ally holds it; while it does not, the group is left out and its boats go to the others. 'stations' are dated changes of its beat: [from turn, sea]. Italy ('ITA'): the rows are [turn, then one count for each group in order: Atlantic, West, Centre, East], on the game's scale of 100 boats in June 1940 and net of the record's losses and new boats. Each beat takes its row's share of the boats Italy's groups actually have that month, so the game's own losses are never counted twice; after the last row its shares hold. The rows: the Mediterranean at 30/40/30 from turn 10 (June 1940), 15/25/20 from 15, 15/30/20 from 24 (it holds in December 1941), 25/25/10 from 39 (sent west against Torch), 15/30/5 from 45; the Atlantic from Bordeaux 8 at turn 13 (September 1940), 18 at 14, 26 at 15, 24 at 19, 27 at 21 (the four Red Sea boats round the Cape), 14 at 24, 11 at 29, 9 at 41 and none from 47 (July 1943), its dated beat the North Atlantic to turn 18 and the Iberian Coast from 19. At stops 1 to 3 the rows are read by date. 'hunts' names the nation whose trade a group hunts ('to') and where the record's boats hunted it, by half-year ('seas': [from turn, seas]; historian/bordeaux-med-subs-b598.md, part 4: west of the British Isles from turn 13, the Azores, Iberian, Canary and Sierra Leone waters from 19, the same southern waters from 25, the American coasts and Brazil from 30 (Operation Neuland, February 1942), Brazil, Freetown and the Cape from 37, the Cape and the Mozambique Channel from 43). At stops 1 to 3 its beat each month is the sea of that half-year's list that carries the most lane feeding that nation while cargoes sail on it (between seas with as much, the first in the list); where every sea in the list carries none, the nearest sea to the list that does (counted outwards from the list's seas; between seas as near, the one with more such lanes, then the first in the chart's order), so that its sinkings fall on that trade where the chart carries it, and never the list's first sea for its own sake (ruling 233 riders b601 and b603: the record's lanes west of Iberia and by the Azores are the sea war's fit after release 1). Only seas within its reach from its port count; its dated beat only where none of them carries such a lane. 'admirals' are dated changes of a group's commander, [from turn, name], at every stop (rider b601: commanders are facts of the day): Bordeaux's Parona to turn 24, Polacchini from 25, Grossi from 40; Germany's local command in the Mediterranean under Donitz, Oehrn from 27, Kreisch from 29, Hartmann from 53. A new commander takes over with a line of news; a group formed after his date forms under him. At stops 4 and 5 the staff places the boats by need (ruling 233 rider b564, as ruling 236 rider b554 moves a staff's budget): each group's beat is the sea within its reach where the enemy's shipping is thickest (the sea lanes and convoy routes through it that feed a nation at war with Italy), its dated beat where none is thicker; the boats start where turn 10's row put them and each month go a sixtieth of the way, about a fifth in a year, towards shares in proportion to that shipping, or towards turn 10's shares where there is none on any beat. (Taken whole at once, the chart's shipping would send every boat to the Atlantic, the one fleet on one beat that rider b562 found wrong.) Need counts lanes only. The enemy's fleets are a target too (rider b598(1)), but a lane and a fleet's weight have no common measure in the rules, so 'floor' holds instead: while a fleet of an enemy's with surface ships has its home port on one of its 'seas' (the Mediterranean's), the groups it names (the three Mediterranean beats), each while its beat is on one of those seas, keep together at least 'least' of the boats, one in three, shared among them as the month's move would share them. A staff at war before turn 10 places them so from its first month of war. Germany ('GER'): the U-boats in the Mediterranean, taken from the fleet 'from' up to as many as it has: rows [turn, West, East], 6 from turn 26 (October 1941, all east), 20 from 28 (east 15, west 5), half west after Torch from 39, 13 from 53 (January 1944, mostly west), none from 61 (September 1944). When a row is lower than what is in the Mediterranean the rest go back to the fleet: play's losses are its own and none is invented. The boats are only lent: a group whose base is lost sends them back too, since Germany may hold no Mediterranean port of its own to move it to. A group left with no boats stands down, and forms again, with its line of news, when it has some. At stops 1 and 2 by date; at stops 3 to 5 only while the record's 'cause' holds: from its turn, an army of a nation in 'by' fighting on the African shore of the Mediterranean ('ground': Libya, Egypt west of Suez, Tunisia and Algeria), at war with a nation that holds ground there.
